title: Your job and your team
summary: Contracting buys what the mission needs, on time, at a fair price, within the law. You do not do it alone: a team of people, each with a lane, gets every requirement from an idea to a delivered product or service.
why: About 9 exam questions test roles and teamwork (Skills and Roles, Team Dynamics), and every other topic assumes you know who does what. On the job, knowing whose decision something is keeps you out of trouble on day one.

sections.h: The people on an acquisition team
sections.body:
- **Requiring activity (the customer):** the unit or office that needs something. They define the requirement and provide the funds.
- **Contract specialist (you):** a 51C or 1102 who does the market research, writes and runs the solicitation, analyzes offers and prepares the contract and its changes. You recommend; the contracting officer decides.
- **Contracting officer (KO):** the warranted official who signs. A KO can be a PCO (procuring), an ACO (administering) or a TCO (terminating). In a contingency, a deployed KO is often called a CCO.
- **Contracting officer's representative (COR):** a customer employee the KO designates in writing to watch the contractor's day-to-day performance. A COR cannot change the contract.
- **Resource manager (RM):** certifies that funds are available on the purchase request.
- **Legal counsel:** reviews larger and riskier actions, protests and claims.
- **Small business professional:** helps decide set-asides and reviews strategies.
- **Program manager:** on bigger programs, owns cost, schedule and performance for the whole effort.

Under the FAR Overhaul, FAR 1.102(a) lists seven guiding principles, in order: meet the agency's mission efficiently and effectively; use taxpayer dollars effectively; buy commercial products and services wherever practicable; award to contractors with a superior ability to perform; compete and give fair opportunity; act with integrity and openness; and push decisions to the lowest appropriate level. Older material still quotes the old vision (best value, public trust, public policy); the exam now tests the RFO wording. Three ideas to remember:
- The acquisition team includes the customer, contracting, finance, legal and the contractor. Everyone is expected to work together.
- The FAR's permission principle: if a strategy or practice is in the Government's best interest and is not prohibited by law, regulation or the FAR, the team may use it (FAR 1.102(b)(4)). The FAR is a framework, not a list of the only things allowed.
- The system manages risk instead of trying to remove it: eliminating all risk would cost taxpayers too much (FAR 1.102(c)).

sections.h: Skills that make a good specialist
sections.body:
- **Business acumen:** understand how companies price, profit and take risk.
- **Problem solving:** focus on the customer's real problem, not just the paperwork.
- **Risk awareness:** spot cost, schedule, performance and legal risk early, and help reduce it.
- **Communication:** short, clear writing; asking good questions; keeping everyone informed.
- **Objectivity:** keep personal bias out of decisions so vendors are treated fairly.

example.title: The printer that was not a printer problem
example.body: A unit asks for 40 new printers, fast. A good specialist asks why. The real problem is that half the old printers lack a maintenance contract. Market research shows a managed print service on an existing contract solves it for less, sooner. The specialist did not just process paperwork: they solved the customer's problem within the rules.

remember: The KO decides and signs; the specialist analyzes and recommends; the COR watches performance; the customer defines the need and pays.
PCO buys it, ACO administers it, TCO terminates it.
mistakes: Letting a COR or customer tell a contractor to do extra work. Only the KO can change a contract.
Treating the customer as an obstacle. They are part of the team, and they know the requirement best.

title: Who can bind the Government
summary: Only a contracting officer acting within the limits of a written warrant can commit the Government to a contract. When anyone else makes a promise to a vendor, it is an unauthorized commitment, and fixing it takes a formal ratification by a senior official.
why: Authority is the foundation of every contract and a favorite exam topic. It is also the most common way new people and customers get the Government into legal and fiscal trouble.

sections.body:
Congress gives agencies the power to contract. The agency head delegates it to the head of the contracting activity (HCA), who appoints contracting officers in writing on an SF 1402, Certificate of Appointment (the warrant). The warrant states the limits, such as a dollar ceiling or the kinds of contracts.

Contracting officers may enter into, administer and terminate contracts only within those limits (FAR 1.402-1). No one else can, no matter their rank or position.

- **Actual authority:** real authority the Government gave the person. It can be express (written in the warrant) or implied (an essential part of the duties actually assigned).
- **Apparent authority:** when it only looks like someone has authority. Unlike in private business, apparent authority does **not** bind the Government. A contractor dealing with the Government is expected to check who has authority.

This is why a commander, program manager, COR or resource manager cannot sign a contract or change one, even with good intentions.

Before signing, the KO must make sure all legal and regulatory requirements are met, funds are available, and the contractor is treated fairly. The KO safeguards the Government's interests and asks for advice from specialists (legal, audit, engineering, finance) when needed (FAR 1.402-2).

example.title: The weekend water line
example.body: On a Saturday a facilities manager calls a plumber to fix a burst pipe and says the Government will pay. Monday the plumber's $14,000 invoice shows up at your office. The manager had no warrant: this is an unauthorized commitment. You do not just pay it. The manager writes up what happened, the office prepares a ratification package with legal review and funding, and the authorized official decides. Your job is to explain the process and the rules, not to make the problem disappear.

remember: No warrant, no deal: apparent authority never binds the Government.
Ratification is the exception, not the plan: it needs a senior official and six conditions.
mistakes: Thinking a commander's or COR's verbal OK makes it legal.
Paying an unauthorized commitment through a new purchase order to make it go away. That hides the problem; ratification is the required route.

title: The rulebook: FAR, DFARS and AFARS
summary: The Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) is the main rulebook for buying with appropriated funds. DoW adds the DFARS, and the Army adds the AFARS. Since 1 February 2026 DoW uses the Revolutionary FAR Overhaul (RFO) versions through class deviations, so numbers you see in older material may have changed.
why: You will look things up every day. The exam expects you to know the FAR part titles and where topics live, and to answer from the RFO-updated FAR and DFARS.

sections.body:
- **FAR** (48 CFR chapter 1): governmentwide rules, 53 parts. Each part covers a topic, such as Part 15, Contracting by Negotiation.
- **DFARS** (48 CFR chapter 2): DoW's supplement. Its parts mirror the FAR's with a 2 in front: DFARS 215 supplements FAR 15.
- **DFARS PGI:** Procedures, Guidance and Information. The how-to that goes with the DFARS; it is not regulation.
- **AFARS** (48 CFR chapter 51): the Army supplement. AFARS 5115 supplements FAR 15.
- Your command may also issue local policies and instructions.

A supplement can add to or tailor the FAR but must not contradict it unless a deviation authorizes it.

A **deviation** is an approved departure from the FAR. An individual deviation covers one action (FAR 1.303); a class deviation covers a category of actions (FAR 1.304).

In 2025 the FAR Council began the **Revolutionary FAR Overhaul (RFO)**: it rewrote each part in plain language, removed many rules not required by law, and renumbered sections. DoW adopted the RFO parts, with matching DFARS changes, through class deviations effective 1 February 2026. The formal rulemaking is still in progress (proposed rules were published in June and September 2026). Until it is finished, the deviation text is what DoW contracting officers use.

Practical effect for you: a section number in an older template, training slide or email may now point somewhere else. When in doubt, check the RFO page on acquisition.gov.

The exam FAQ says to know the titles of FAR Parts 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 12, 13, 15, 16, 19, 31, 33, 42, 44, 46 and 49. Use the Flashcards deck and the FAR Part Match game until you can say each title from its number and each number from its title.

example.title: The old template
example.body: A teammate hands you a sole-source justification template that cites FAR 6.302-1. Under the RFO, that authority is now FAR 6.103-1, and the approval rules moved from 6.304 to 6.104-2 (with DoW's own approval table in DFARS 206.104-71). You update the cites and check the current approval levels before routing it.

remember: FAR + 200 = DFARS part; FAR + 5100 = AFARS part.
mistakes: Trusting a cite in an old template without checking the RFO page.
Treating PGI or a local policy as if it overrides the FAR.

title: What makes a contract
summary: A contract is a legally binding agreement. It needs an offer, an acceptance, consideration (something of value each way), parties with the authority and capacity to agree, and a lawful purpose. The Government also uses grants, cooperative agreements and other transactions, which are not contracts.
why: Contract formation questions show up across the exam, and you need them to understand why quotes, purchase orders and awards work the way they do.

sections.body:
- **Offer:** a promise to do something on stated terms, which the other side can accept.
- **Acceptance:** agreement to the offer's terms. A response that changes the terms is a counteroffer, not an acceptance.
- **Consideration:** each side gives something of value: the contractor delivers, the Government pays.
- **Competent parties with authority:** for the Government, a contracting officer acting within the warrant.
- **Lawful purpose:** the Government can only contract for what the law allows, using funds available for that purpose.

In a request for quotations (RFQ), a vendor's quote is **not** an offer; it is information. The Government's purchase order is the offer, and a contract forms when the vendor accepts it in writing or by starting to perform (FAR 12.201-1(b)).

In a request for proposals (RFP) or an invitation for bids (IFB), the contractor's proposal or bid is the offer, and the Government's award is the acceptance.

sections.h: Contract, grant, cooperative agreement or other transaction?
sections.body:
The law decides which instrument fits (31 U.S.C. 6303 to 6305):
- **Contract:** the Government buys property or services for its own direct benefit or use.
- **Grant:** the Government transfers money to carry out a public purpose, with little Government involvement.
- **Cooperative agreement:** like a grant, but with substantial Government involvement.
- **Other transaction (OT):** a flexible instrument used under specific laws, such as prototype projects (10 U.S.C. 4022). OTs are not governed by the FAR.

Contracting officers handle contracts; grants and agreements officers handle the others.

- **Purchase order:** a simple contract, often under the simplified acquisition threshold.
- **Definitive contract:** a complete contract with all terms agreed.
- **Order under an existing contract:** a delivery order (supplies) or task order (services) placed under an indefinite-delivery contract.
- **Blanket purchase agreement (BPA)** and **basic ordering agreement (BOA):** agreements that set terms in advance. They are not contracts by themselves; each call or order is.

example.title: The changed quote
example.body: You send a purchase order for 100 radios at the quoted price. The vendor writes back: 'Accepted, but delivery will be 60 days, not 30.' That is a counteroffer, not an acceptance. There is no contract until both sides agree on the same terms.

remember: Offer + acceptance + consideration + authority + lawful purpose.
In simplified buys the PO is the offer; in RFPs the proposal is the offer.
mistakes: Calling a BPA a contract. Each call under it is the contract.
Assuming a quote binds the vendor. It does not.

title: Money rules: Purpose, Time and Amount
summary: Appropriated money can be used only for the purpose Congress gave it, only during the period it is available, and only up to the amount provided. Breaking these rules can violate the Antideficiency Act, which carries penalties for the people involved.
why: Funds questions appear under contract principles and planning. On the job, the contracting officer may not sign a contract without available funds, and fiscal mistakes are among the most serious you can make.

sections.body: Funds may be spent only for the objects Congress appropriated them for (31 U.S.C. 1301(a)). The test: the expense must be logically related to the appropriation, not prohibited by law, and not covered by a more specific appropriation. Example: operation and maintenance (O&M) money cannot build a new building that should be military construction.

An appropriation can pay only for a **bona fide need** of the period it is available (31 U.S.C. 1502(a)). Typical DoW availability periods:
- O&M: 1 year
- Research, development, test and evaluation (RDT&E): 2 years
- Procurement: 3 years
- Military construction: 5 years

After that, funds expire and can be used only to adjust or pay existing obligations for 5 more years, then they cancel.

**Services:** severable services (like recurring maintenance) are a need of the year performed. DoW may still fund up to 12 months of severable services that start in one fiscal year with that year's funds (10 U.S.C. 3133). Non-severable services (one end product, like a study) are funded entirely when the need arises.

Check that the purchase request is certified, that the appropriation fits the purpose and the fiscal year, and that the dollar amount covers the award. When something looks wrong, stop and ask the resource manager or legal counsel before you sign anything.

example.title: End-of-year money
example.body: On 25 September a customer offers expiring FY O&M funds to buy next year's office supplies and a service contract that starts in January. The supplies are not a need of this year, so buying them with this year's money violates the bona fide needs rule. The service contract starting in January is a need of next fiscal year (which starts 1 October), so this year's funds are the wrong funds for it.

remember: Purpose, Time, Amount: the three legs of fiscal law.
mistakes: Signing a modification first and finding funds later.
Using expiring funds to stock up for next year.

title: Ethics and integrity
summary: Contracting runs on public trust. Treat every vendor fairly, protect the information you are trusted with, avoid conflicts of interest and even the appearance of them, and report wrongdoing. Breaking these rules can end careers and lead to criminal charges.
why: Standards of Conduct is a full exam competency (6 questions), and your integrity is the one thing you cannot rebuild once it is gone.

sections.body: Government business must be conducted above reproach, with complete impartiality and preferential treatment for none. Avoid any conflict of interest, and avoid even the appearance of one (FAR 3.101).

The Procurement Integrity Act (41 U.S.C. 2101 to 2107, implemented in FAR 3.104):
- You may not disclose **contractor bid or proposal information** or **source selection information** before award to anyone not authorized to see it.
- No one may obtain such information improperly.
- If you are participating personally and substantially in a buy over the simplified acquisition threshold and an offeror contacts you about employment, you must report it and either reject the offer or recuse yourself.
- Some former officials face limits on taking pay from a contractor after certain decisions.

Federal ethics rules (5 CFR 2635) generally prohibit accepting gifts from people who do business with your agency. Small exceptions exist (such as items of modest value), but as a contracting professional the safest answer is to decline and ask your ethics counselor. Contractors are also barred from offering gratuities to get favorable treatment (FAR 3.2).

- **Kickbacks:** payments to get a subcontract or favorable treatment are illegal (FAR 3.502).
- **Bid rigging and collusion:** report signs of it, such as identical bids or rotating winners, through legal counsel (FAR 3.303).
- **Organizational conflicts of interest:** a contractor's other work could bias its advice or give it an unfair edge (FAR 9.5).
- **Personal conflicts of interest** of contractor employees who do acquisition work for the Government (FAR 3.11).
- **Whistleblowers:** contractor employees who report wrongdoing are protected (FAR 3.9).

Stop. Do not proceed with the action. Write down what you know, and tell your contracting officer, supervisor or legal counsel. You can also report fraud, waste and abuse to the Inspector General hotline.

example.title: Lunch with an incumbent
example.body: Two weeks before proposals are due, the incumbent's program manager invites you to lunch 'to talk about the requirement.' Meeting would give one competitor information and access others did not get, and the lunch itself is a gift from a prohibited source. You decline politely and tell them to submit questions in writing to the contracting officer, so the answers can go to everyone.

remember: Above reproach, impartial, and no preferential treatment for anyone.
When in doubt, do not: stop and ask the ethics counselor.
mistakes: Sharing the IGCE or another firm's price 'to help' a vendor.
Answering one vendor's question without giving the same answer to all.

title: Write it down: the contract file
summary: If it is not in the file, it did not happen. The contract file must tell the complete story of an acquisition so that someone who was not there can understand every decision and why it was made.
why: Communication and documentation is an exam competency of its own, and good files are what protect you, your contracting officer and the Government in audits, protests and lawsuits.

sections.body:
Every office that does contracting, contract administration or payment keeps a file for each solicitation and contract action. The file must comprehensively record the transaction history: the background for decisions, the support for actions taken, information for reviews and investigations, and essential facts for litigation or congressional inquiries (FAR 4.101).

The Army keeps contract files electronically in the Virtual Contracting Enterprise (VCE) Paperless Contract File, following AFARS and its PGI.

- **Memorandum for record (MFR):** what happened, when, who decided, and why.
- **Determination and findings (D&F):** a formal written approval: the findings (facts) support the determination (decision). Some actions require one, such as soliciting only one source on a noncommercial simplified buy (FAR 13.101(b)). Under the RFO, the rules for D&Fs are in FAR Subpart 1.5.
- **Price reasonableness determination**, market research report, acquisition plan, source selection documents, negotiation memorandum, and more.

Write so a stranger can follow it: dates, names or roles, numbers, and the reasoning that connects the facts to the decision.

- Lead with the bottom line, then the support.
- Use the same terms the contract uses; do not invent new ones.
- Put agreements with contractors in writing. A phone call that changes something must end with a written record and, if it changes the contract, a modification.
- Keep internal advice (pre-decisional notes, legal advice) separate from what you release.
- Remember that emails are records and can be requested in litigation or under FOIA.

The competency model also expects you to look at each new requirement in its context: the customer's mission, the market, past problems and the risks. After each action, capture lessons learned so the next buy goes better, and share them with your team.

example.title: The missing why
example.body: An auditor asks why a $90,000 buy went to the second-lowest quote. The file has three quotes and the purchase order, nothing else. The specialist remembers the low quote could not meet the delivery date, but nobody wrote it down. A two-line memo at the time would have closed the question in seconds.

remember: If it is not in the file, it did not happen.
Facts, decision, reason, date, who: in every memo.
mistakes: Leaving key decisions in email threads instead of the file.
Writing memos only the author can understand.

title: Rights and remedies in every contract
summary: Every contract spreads rights and risks between the Government and the contractor through its clauses: when the Government inspects and accepts, who owns the goods and bears the loss, what counts as an excusable delay, how payment works, and how changes and terminations happen.
why: Contract Principles is the largest single competency on the exam (18 questions). These ideas come back in pre-award, award and post-award questions.

sections.body: The Government has the right to inspect and test what it buys. **Acceptance** is the act of the authorized Government representative taking ownership of supplies or approving services. Once accepted, it is final and conclusive, except for latent defects, fraud, gross mistakes amounting to fraud, or as the contract otherwise provides, such as a warranty (FAR 46.5).

Who owns the goods, and who pays if they are lost or damaged in transit, depends on the delivery terms. Under **f.o.b. origin**, the Government takes risk when the goods leave the seller; under **f.o.b. destination**, the seller keeps the risk until delivery (FAR 47.303; risk of loss, FAR 46.505).

A contractor is not in default for a delay caused by events beyond its control and without its fault or negligence, such as acts of God, acts of the Government, fires, floods, epidemics, quarantine restrictions, strikes, freight embargoes and unusually severe weather (52.249-14, Excusable Delays). Other delays can lead to termination for default.

- The Prompt Payment Act requires payment generally within 30 days of a proper invoice or acceptance, whichever is later; late payment brings automatic interest (FAR 32.9).
- A **warranty** is a promise about the quality or performance of what is delivered. It gives the Government remedies after acceptance. Warranties cost money, so use them when the benefit is worth it (FAR 46.7).

- The **Changes** clause lets the contracting officer order changes within the general scope of the contract; the contractor must keep working and can get an equitable adjustment (FAR 43.3, 52.243-1).
- The Government can end a contract for its **convenience** (paying for work done) or for **default** when the contractor fails to perform (FAR Part 49).
- **Repudiation:** a clear statement that a party will not perform, which can be treated as a breach.

example.title: Damaged in transit
example.body: Generators shipped f.o.b. origin arrive damaged after a trucking accident. Because risk passed to the Government when the generators left the seller's dock, the Government files the claim against the carrier; the seller still gets paid. Under f.o.b. destination, the seller would have borne the loss and owed undamaged generators.

remember: Acceptance is final except for latent defects, fraud, gross mistakes amounting to fraud, or a warranty.
Origin: Government owns the trip. Destination: seller owns the trip.
mistakes: Assuming acceptance can always be undone later.
Telling a contractor a delay is excusable before the facts are known.
